The post Baseten Releases joey-1, a 2B Decision Model at $0.01 per 1M Tokens appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Baseten has released joey-1 , a 2B model from its in-house research lab, Base Labs. The joey-1 decision model returns a label and a calibrated probability instead of generated text. It targets high-volume routing, classification and guardrail checks. Baseten prices it at $0.01 per million input tokens , with open weights on Hugging Face under MIT. TL;DR Size: 2B parameters, post-trained from Qwen3.5-2B. 16,384-token max sequence (Baseten says 262k on dedicated deployments). Runs on: Baseten Model APIs, or self-hosted on 1 CUDA GPU (VRAM not disclosed). No official quantized builds listed. Performance: Top model under 4B on the Jev Decision Index 0.4 public split, per Baseten. Best: 63.30 on Jev Decision Index 0.4 (public split), ranked #37 of 230 models. Worst: Trails its 9B sibling elephant-1 by 8.94 points on the same split (63.30 vs 72.24). Bottom line: Best: 20 ms P50 decisions for $0.01 per 1M tokens. Worst: less general knowledge than its larger siblings. What is joey-1? joey-1 is a 2B decision model from Baseten’s Base Labs that answers typed questions in 1 forward pass. You send a state (text or images) and 1 or more questions. The model returns a probability for every option of every question. It does not write free-form text that your application must parse. It supports 3 question types: choice: pick 1 named option, such as which team owns a ticket. yes/no ( noul in the API): returns the probability of yes. score: ordered levels, lowest first, such as urgency. joey-1 is the third member of a family. Baseten shipped mammoth-1 (27B) and elephant-1 (9B) last week. All 3 share training data and the /v1/systemone API, so switching is a 1-line change. How does joey-1 work? Base Labs post-trained Qwen3.5-2B with a full fine-tune of the language model. The vision encoder stays frozen. Full-attention layers use a block-bidirectional mask. All questions are answered from 1 shared-prefix prefill, so extra questions add little cost. Training details from the model card : Data: 6.21M decision examples. Mix: 58.3% core decision skills, 16.1% safety, 16.1% judging and expert domains, 9.5% public data. Objective: cross-entropy plus a Brier calibration term, with a trained “I don’t know” option. Recipe: 1 epoch, 43,390 steps, peak learning rate 1e-5, bf16. Hardware: 2 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. Calibration lets you set a confidence threshold. Uncertain answers can escalate to elephant-1, mammoth-1 or a human. How fast and cheap is joey-1? Baseten reports a P50 end-to-end latency of 20 ms for an average 2,000-token request. That is about 2.5x faster than elephant-1 (49 ms). The blog’s TL;DR also claims 5x faster than comparable decision models, without naming them. Model APIs charge $0.01 per 1M input tokens; output and cached input are listed at $0.00. elephant-1 costs $0.035 and mammoth-1 costs $0.10. Baseten’s example: 10M support tickets a month at about 500 tokens each is 5B tokens. That is about $50 on joey-1, versus $500 on mammoth-1. How does joey-1 score on benchmarks? All scores below are self-reported on Baseten’s model card . On the Jev Decision Index 0.4 public split, joey-1 scores 63.30. That ranks #37 of 230 models and is the top score under 4B. The Jev Decision Index is a community leaderboard on Hugging Face. On the same split, Cloudflare’s 27B Clef scores 61.71 and Jev 1.14 scores 60.70. joey-1 trails elephant-1 in every area. It beats Jev 1.14 in 4 of 5 areas, including language, tools and retrieval. It scores 58.9% on FrontierFinance at $0.61 per question, beating Claude Fable 5.1’s 55.9% at $6.89. The post Samaya AI Releases Sterling: A 3B-Active Finance Research Agent Model that Beats Claude Fable 5.1 on FrontierFinance at 11x Lower Cost appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Samaya AI has released Samaya Sterling , a post-trained model for agentic financial research. Sterling is built on NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning , a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. On Samaya’s FrontierFinance benchmark , it scores 58.9%. Claude Fable 5.1 scores 55.9%. Each Sterling question costs $0.61, against $6.89 for Fable 5.1. For developers, the takeaway is a concrete recipe: co-train a small model with its harness, and it can win in a narrow domain. TL;DR Size: 30B total, 3B active (MoE). Base model context: up to 1M tokens. Sterling’s serving context: not disclosed. Runs on: the base model fits a single H100 80GB in BF16 (256K context). Sterling’s serving hardware: not disclosed. Performance: beats every high-quality system on the FrontierFinance leaderboard on quality per dollar (self-reported). Best: 58.9% on FrontierFinance (60.6% in high-effort mode), vs 55.9% for Claude Fable 5.1. Worst: 45.2% on the hardest third of FrontierFinance questions. What is Samaya Sterling? Samaya Sterling is a LoRA post-trained version of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, tuned to work as a financial research agent. It plans research, calls finance tools, gathers evidence and hands findings to a separate report writer. According to Maithra Raghu’s X announcement , it started as a 2-person effort on agentic orchestration efficiency. How does the harness support a 3B-active model? Samaya team adapted its production finance harness for a small model. Detailed guidance was stripped from the system prompt and tool descriptions. Tools were merged to shorten the prompt. Two helper models manage context. A condenser shortens long tool results. A compactor summarizes the trace as it grows. A research budget caps how long the agent works. After that, the report writer answers from what was found. How was Sterling trained? Training used LoRA on Tinker , Thinking Machines Lab’s training API. It ran in 4 stages: SFT on synthetic traces : Samaya generated 968 synthetic analyst questions. The teacher, Kimi K3, answered each twice, and an LLM judge picked the better answer. The model learned to call 37 tools with valid arguments. SFT on the best of 8 strategies : Kimi K3 answered 1,819 expert-written questions using 8 research strategies. The best-graded answer per question became training data. Best-of-8 met 80% of essential rubric items, against about 66% for the single best strategy. After filtering, 1,157 questions remained. Offline GRPO : GRPO scored all 8 teacher answers against each other. No new generation was needed, so each step was cheap. Online GRPO : The model answered each question 8 times and learned from graded attempts. Truncated importance sampling corrected a known MoE sampler mismatch. How does Sterling score on FrontierFinance? FrontierFinance has 220 public queries scored against expert-written rubrics. The grader uses a 3-model judge panel. Samaya team states that no benchmark question was used in training. Checkpoints were chosen on 100 internal validation questions. Sterling scores 58.9% at $0.61 and 282 s per question. Fable 5.1 scores 55.9% at $6.89 and 268 s. Samaya’s own high-effort system scores 2.9 points lower at $1.81. Every stage added quality: 42.5% (base), 51.4%, 54.8%, 57.5%, then 58.9%. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Thu, 29 Oct 2026 17:37:15 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Sector Snapshot: Travel Tech Funding Heads Toward Multiyear Low Despite AI Push https://news.crunchbase.com/travel-tourism/travel-tech-startup-venture-funding-low-ai/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 11:00:49 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94304 Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question. Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech. The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count. AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning. The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019. Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.” Notable deals Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States. The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews , which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth , with participation from Atomico , HarbourVest Partners , Kinnevik , Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management . The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion. Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities , joined by New Alliance Capital , Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely , develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis. Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue. Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field , bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million. Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo , which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital , Isai and Ternel . The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments. Exits Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities. Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets , a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February. On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November. Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing. Point data providers are moving up the stack. Workflow and enrichment tools are repositioning as operating systems. Buyers are assembling their own stacks from components that used to be bought as a platform. Knowing what each competitor shipped last quarter is table stakes — the job is understanding what the pattern means and what we should do about it.</p> <p>This role owns competitive intelligence and win/loss for 6sense. It sits on the Product Marketing team and exists so that our positioning, our roadmap conversations and our field enablement are built on evidence rather than assumption. You will be the person the company turns to when there is a disagreement about why we win, why we lose, and who we are actually competing against.</p> <p>This is a senior individual contributor seat. The work is research, synthesis and judgment — and the willingness to tell the company something it would rather not hear, with the evidence to back it up.</p> <hr> <h2>What You'll Own</h2> <ul> <li> <p><strong>The win/loss program, end to end.</strong> Interviews, coding, synthesis and the readouts that go to product and executive leadership.
